# MySQL application database

## Use when

Use this pattern when an application deliberately chooses MySQL or MariaDB.
Install `@jskit-ai/database-runtime` and `@jskit-ai/database-runtime-mysql`
without a package-setup wizard: the runtime brings Knex and the driver brings
`mysql2`. The driver takes the runtime as a peer, so the application holds its
one copy.

## Do not use when

Do not use this pattern for PostgreSQL, a database-neutral library, or a service
that does not own its database connection. Do not install both JSKIT drivers
unless the application genuinely selects between them at runtime.

## Product decisions

Decide the database name, credentials, host, deployment secret source, backup
policy, and application migrations. Those are application and environment
decisions, not framework questions.

## Invariants

- The application depends directly on the selected JSKIT driver.
- Credentials stay outside Git.
- `knexfile.js` fixes `mysql2`; a single-driver application does not require
  `DB_CLIENT`.
- Schema changes are ordinary immutable migrations.
- The current package graph, environment, and migrations are authoritative.

## Framework APIs

Use `createKnexMigrationConfigFromApp()` from
`@jskit-ai/database-runtime/server/knexMigrationConfig`, and
`prepareDatabaseFromApp()` from `@jskit-ai/database-runtime/server/databaseSetup`.
Both take the dialect and the application's environment
(`environment: process.env`), which they never read on their own. The running JSKIT
application automatically selects the sole installed database driver, while
Knex discovers package-owned migrations from the installed dependency graph.

## Example files

`example/package.json` contains the runtime dependency and database scripts.
`example/knexfile.js` loads an optional local `.env` and fixes the MySQL dialect.
`example/scripts/prepare-database.js` is the portable migrate-then-seed
entrypoint for managed sessions and deployments. It loads the optional `.env`
as the knexfile does, and migrates the database `DB_NAME` names without
creating it: the hosting environment or a database administrator creates it
first. `example/.env.example` names the connection values and separate test
databases without a secret.

`example/.github/workflows/verify.yml` is a normal app-owned CI workflow with
exactly one database service: `mariadb` (`mariadb:11.4`, `MARIADB_*`
variables, port `3306`, a `healthcheck.sh` health check). Copy it whole from
this pattern and adapt it as source rather than generating it from package
metadata. Do not combine it with the PostgreSQL pattern's workflow: a MySQL
application's workflow has no `postgres` service, `POSTGRES_*` variables, port
`5432`, or `pg_isready` option.

Tests get their own databases from
`@jskit-ai/database-runtime/server/testDatabases`. The `test` script runs
`jskit test --databases`: each Node test file running at once gets its own
copy of `TEST_DB_NAME` (`<name>`, `<name>_1`, ...), restored from a stored
snapshot of the current migrations' schema and the rows they write, in
`node_modules/.cache/jskit-test-databases/`. The snapshot is replayed once, and
again only when a migration's name or contents or `package-lock.json` change;
a file that migrates or drops tables leaves its copy to be restored before the
next file takes it.

`example/tests/e2e/databases.js` is the browser run's `prepare` module for
`browserTestConfig({ prepare: "tests/e2e/databases.js" })` from
`@jskit-ai/jskit-catalog/browser-tests`. It gives each Playwright worker's
server its own copy of `BROWSER_TEST_DB_NAME`, restored from the same kind of
snapshot and seeded in one transaction by the app's fixture `seed`, which
restores any migration-owned baseline rows the app needs. Every server serves
the production build. Both refuse the application's database (`DB_NAME`,
`DATABASE_URL`'s, the Knex connection's), `PROD_DB_NAME` and the other test
database and its copies. Provision `TEST_DB_NAME`, `BROWSER_TEST_DB_NAME` and
their numbered copies with grants for the application account (a `<app>_%`
grant covers them); a user who may create no copies runs one file or worker at
a time. Two test runs at once need different database names. Test-only server
settings that disable external effects (email, payments) go in
`browserTestConfig({ env })`; a suite that writes data proves the server's
identity first.

Each preparation reports how many databases it made, whether it replayed the
migrations for a new snapshot, and the restore and seed durations. Use those
measurements to diagnose a slow start before rerunning a browser case.

Keep fixtures small for the selected test scope. Run related cases in one suite
invocation. Fresh-schema migration proofs are separate from browser startup.

## Variation points

Change scripts, migration location, connection values, and secret injection to
fit the application. Supply `DATABASE_URL` instead of individual values when
the environment owns a URL. Add `DB_CLIENT=mysql2` only when a shared external
tool explicitly needs a dialect selector. When the product needs initial data,
import one idempotent app-owned seed function in `prepare-database.js` and pass
it as `seed` to `prepareDatabaseFromApp()`.

## Verification

- Install dependencies once with `npm install`.
- Run `npm run db:prepare` against a fresh disposable database.
- Run `npm run db:migrate:status` and the application verification command.
- Exercise one transaction and one negative connection case.
- When a seed exists, run `db:prepare` twice and require the second run to be safe.
- For the test databases, run the suite twice: the second run restores the
  stored snapshot instead of replaying the migrations, stale rows are gone,
  baseline rows are restored, foreign keys are enforced, and the normal
  database is unchanged. A new migration takes a new snapshot.
- Confirm `.github/workflows/verify.yml` parses as YAML and declares only the
  `mariadb` service. GitHub reports an unparseable workflow only as a failed
  run with "no jobs were run".

## Avoid

- framework questionnaires for credentials
- generated `.env` secrets
- depending on a live schema as the source contract
- a second driver installed “just in case”
- any file, service, port, or variable copied from the PostgreSQL pattern
- migration receipts, provenance, replay logs, or generator ownership
